clue.text: "Whose —— are alternate Night and Day" (O. Khayyam)

definitions.text: "Whose —— are alternate Night and Day" (O. Khayyam)

parts.words: "Whose —— are alternate Night and Day" (O. Khayyam)
parts.note: a line from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, describing the world as an inn whose doorways are day and night; the solver supplies the missing word

explanation.surface: A quotation from the Rubaiyat with one word left blank for the solver.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a dash after 'Whose' for the gap: the Rubaiyat calls the world a battered caravanserai whose doorways are alternate Night and Day.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand doorways or gateways, the entrances of the poem's caravanserai, fill the gap in the line.

clue.text: Some writing has equal value with a diagram

parts.note: two things at par are of equal value
a graph is a diagram plotting values

explanation.surface: A piece of text is worth as much as a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A section of prose set off by a new line is a portion of a piece of text.

clue.text: The Frenchman's revolutionary dream should be respected

parts.note: reve is French for a dream, as 'The Frenchman's' signals
a revolutionary is a red, a communist

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's dream of revolution deserves esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Frenchman's' tells us to give 'dream' in French, REVE, which then comes before RED for 'revolutionary'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be held in deep esteem is to be venerated, honoured.

clue.text: There should be a love grant for this giver-up

indicators.note: the clue's opening tells us the following letters should be made into the word, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
love is nil in tennis, the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grant of love ought to go to someone self-denying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There should' asks for the letters of BE A O GRANT to be rearranged into the word, with 'love' giving O.
explanation.definitionFit: One who renounces or gives up something is a self-denier, from the verb abnegate.

clue.text: A villeinous character

parts.note: villein, a feudal tenant bound to the land, is spelt like a pun on villainous

explanation.surface: A wicked person in a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Villeinous' is not 'villainous': a villein was a medieval peasant tied to his lord's land.
explanation.definitionFit: A villein was a feudal bondman, an unfree labourer bound to the manor.

clue.text: The gardener's best policy

parts.note: the proverb about truthfulness being the best policy, combined with the garden plant of the same name with silvery seed pods

explanation.surface: Advice on how a gardener should conduct business.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb says truthfulness is the best policy; the gardener's version is a cottage-garden plant, Lunaria, grown for its papery moon-like seed discs.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant Lunaria shares its name with the virtue of truthfulness in the proverb.

clue.text: Hasten, Mars, to produce this annoying tactic

indicators.note: the two names are worked over to produce something new, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An appeal to the war god to hurry and create a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to produce' asks for the letters of HASTEN MARS to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Persistent pestering or intimidation is a tactic designed to annoy and wear down.

clue.text: The diminutive Henrietta is coming up at ten

indicators.note: in a down clue the words climbing upward are read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Little Henrietta arrives at ten o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns AT TEN in this down light, giving a pet form of Henrietta.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet form of a girl's name is a shortened version of it.

clue.text: Singular or plural Moslem confraternity

parts.note: a North African Sufi brotherhood founded in 1837, whose name serves for one member or for the order

explanation.surface: A grammar note on a Muslim religious brotherhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The Senussi order, founded in Libya, uses one word for a member and for all; 'Moslem' is an older spelling of Muslim.
explanation.definitionFit: The Libyan Sufi order founded by Muhammad ibn Ali al-Senussi is a Muslim brotherhood.

clue.text: Want to hear a story about the Orient ?

indicators.note: a story goes about, round, the Orient letter

parts.note: a yarn is a tale
the Orient is the East, E

explanation.surface: Eager to listen to a tale of the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts E (the East) inside YARN.
explanation.definitionFit: To long or crave for something is to feel desire for it.

clue.text: One of Elijah's desert commissariat

parts.note: in 1 Kings 17 the prophet Elijah, hiding by the brook Cherith, was fed bread and meat by black birds

explanation.surface: A member of the supply corps that fed a prophet in the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: A commissariat is an army's food-supply department; the black birds that brought Elijah food served as his.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible says black corvid birds carried bread and flesh to the prophet each morning and evening.

clue.text: Country song of Proms fame — but Ichabod !

indicators.note: Ichabod is the biblical cry 'the glory is departed', so some of the song title's letters are told to depart

parts.note: Rule, Britannia! is sung every year at the Last Night of the Proms in London

explanation.surface: A patriotic song famous from the Proms, with a lament that the glory has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ichabod' (1 Samuel 4: 'the glory is departed') removes L, E, B and one N from RULE BRITANNIA, leaving the fictional kingdom of Anthony Hope's novels; the Proms are London's summer concert season.
explanation.definitionFit: The imaginary Central European kingdom of The Prisoner of Zenda is a nation in fiction.

clue.text: Artist, gloved, in car place

annotationWithheld.why: Artist, gloved, in car place (6): RA inside GAGE (a glove thrown down as a challenge) gives GARAGE, but 'gloved' must both supply GAGE and signal the insertion, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Hashish-eater devoted to the Old Man of the Mountains

definitions.meaning: the word comes from the Arabic hashshashin, users of hashish

definitions.text: devoted to the Old Man of the Mountains
definitions.meaning: the medieval Nizari sect, followers of the Old Man of the Mountains, Hasan-i Sabbah, were famed killers

explanation.surface: A drug user who follows a mysterious mountain sheikh.
explanation.definitionFit: The word for a political murderer derives from the hashish-using followers of the Old Man of the Mountains.

clue.text: How the workshy operate with canvas on the leg

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece sits on top of the other

parts.note: scrim is a light open-weave canvas
the shank is the leg, from knee to ankle

explanation.surface: Lazy workers wrapping a bandage round the leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' sets SCRIM above SHANK in the down light; the result is British military slang for dodging work.
explanation.definitionFit: British service slang for shirking duty describes the shirker's way of working.

clue.text: Ale in the academic sense

parts.note: Oxford and Cambridge colleges brewed a strong beer for the day tenants paid their accounts, named for that inspection of accounts

explanation.surface: A definition of beer as scholars understand it.
explanation.walkthrough: Audit ale was a strong ale brewed by Oxbridge colleges for audit day, when accounts were settled; in the academic sense 'ale' takes this word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: College account-checking day gave its name to a special strong beer.

clue.text: Hence loathed Melancholy … In dark —— desert ever dwell" (Milton)

definitions.text: Hence loathed Melancholy … In dark —— desert ever dwell" (Milton)

parts.words: Hence loathed Melancholy … In dark —— desert ever dwell" (Milton)
parts.note: the opening of Milton's L'Allegro, banishing Melancholy to a dark desert named after a mythical people living in perpetual gloom

explanation.surface: A quotation from Milton with one word left blank for the solver.
explanation.walkthrough: In Homer the Cimmerians live at the edge of the world in endless darkness, so Milton sends Melancholy to their gloomy desert.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the mythical land of perpetual night where Homer placed a people beyond the sun.

clue.text: Cut it out !

parts.note: read not as a demand to stop but as an instruction to remove something

explanation.surface: An exasperated order to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation sounds like 'stop that!', but read as an instruction it means remove it.
explanation.definitionFit: To remove or get rid of something entirely is to excise it.

clue.text: E. Lear's ESP faculties ?

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote books of absurd verse

explanation.surface: Asking whether Edward Lear had psychic powers.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear's Book of Nonsense supplies one reading; extrasensory perception is a set of faculties that are 'non-senses'.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear's absurd verses are pieces of silliness, while extrasensory powers lie beyond the senses.

clue.text: Irish-Scottish contestant in the field

definitions.meaning: Hibernia is the Latin name for Ireland, so its adjective means of Ireland
an Edinburgh football club competing on the pitch, or one of its players

explanation.surface: A sportsman with both Irish and Scottish roots.
explanation.walkthrough: Hibernian is an Edinburgh football club founded by Irish immigrants, so the name covers both halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin Hibernia means Ireland, and the Edinburgh football club Hibs takes that name.

clue.text: Captain Bobadil, for one

parts.note: the cowardly braggart soldier in Ben Jonson's Every Man in His Humour

explanation.surface: A character offered as an example of a type.
explanation.walkthrough: Bobadil, in Ben Jonson's comedy Every Man in His Humour, is a vainglorious soldier full of tall tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonson's Bobadil is the stock braggart, a man who brags of his valour.

clue.text: Model of 5 ac.

parts.note: 5 across is truthfulness, and the old schoolboy oath 'Honest ...' names a model of it

explanation.surface: A cross-reference asking for the very pattern of an earlier answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honest Injun' was an old schoolboy oath swearing truthfulness, so this word stands as the model of 5 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The schoolboy oath pairs this dated word with honest, making it an emblem of truthfulness.

clue.text: An Austen fan of Kipling's

parts.note: Kipling's short story The ... tells of soldiers who idolise Jane Austen's novels

explanation.surface: A Jane Austen admirer in one of Kipling's stories.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling coined the name in his 1924 story about First World War gunners devoted to Jane Austen's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: A devotee of Jane Austen is named after her first name, popularised by Kipling's story.

clue.text: Extremely forward chief gets the majority

parts.note: a chief is a head, the leader of a group
the majority is the most, the greater part

explanation.surface: A forceful leader takes the bulk of the votes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something placed furthest forward is at the very front, a superlative of forward position.

clue.text: Laughter on the boundaries

definitions.meaning: a ha-ha is a sunken ditch and wall marking an estate's edge without blocking the view

explanation.surface: Merriment heard around the edges of a field.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunken fence in English landscape gardens shares its name with laughs.

clue.text: Language of a famed proposal to the owl.?

definitions.text: Language of a famed proposal to the owl.?

parts.words: Language of a famed proposal to the owl.?
parts.note: in Lear's The Owl and the Pussy-cat the cat would answer the owl's proposal in its own tongue

explanation.surface: Asking how a famous marriage proposal to an owl was phrased.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lear's poem the owl woos the Pussy-cat; a cat's language is its mew, so this is what she would reply in.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat's mewing call is its language in reply to the owl.

clue.text: Perpetual moaner in the Second World War

definitions.text: Perpetual moaner in the Second World War

parts.words: Perpetual moaner in the Second World War
parts.note: British troops named a German multi-barrelled mortar after its wailing shells, and the phrase 'moaning ...' also means a chronic complainer

explanation.surface: A soldier who never stopped complaining during the war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moaning Minnie' was the British nickname for the German Nebelwerfer mortar and for air-raid sirens; it later came to mean a habitual grumbler.
explanation.definitionFit: The wailing German rocket mortar of the war was nicknamed Moaning followed by this girl's name.

clue.text: Luxury House of Correction ?

parts.note: a luxury rooftop flat is a ..., and a house of correction confines its inmates

explanation.surface: A prison with five-star comforts.
explanation.walkthrough: Add 'house' to the answer and you get a luxury flat; a house of correction keeps people shut up.
explanation.definitionFit: Inmates of a prison are confined, shut in, and the word plus house names a luxury apartment.

clue.text: "The March of the Gladiators" for the Top Twenty?

definitions.text: The March of the Gladiators" for the Top Twenty?

parts.words: The March of the Gladiators" for the Top Twenty?
parts.note: gladiators striking blows while marching would make a procession of blows, also the name of a chart of best-selling records

explanation.surface: Fucik's circus march put forward for the pop charts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Entry of the Gladiators is a famous circus march; fighters who strike blows parade, and the best-seller chart of the day carried the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The weekly chart of the best-selling records was called by this name, punned as a procession of blows.

clue.text: A girl goes wrong

parts.note: a miss is a young unmarried woman

explanation.surface: A young woman strays into bad ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gone awry is faulty or out of order, the predicative sense of wrong.

clue.text: Island domain of an old British rajah

definitions.text: Island domain of an old British rajah

parts.words: Island domain of an old British rajah
parts.note: James Brooke, an Englishman, became the White Rajah of a state on Borneo, ruled by his family until 1946

explanation.surface: The territory an Englishman once ruled as rajah on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Brooke family, the 'White Rajahs', ruled this state on the island of Borneo from 1841 to 1946.
explanation.definitionFit: The Borneo state ruled by the Brooke family of White Rajahs is the island domain meant.

clue.text: Uncle Sam's seesaws start on the course

definitions.meaning: Americans call a seesaw a teeter-totter, or a teeter
on a golf course the start of each hole is the tee, and those who drive off from it are read as tee-ers

explanation.surface: American playground seesaws set up at the opening of a golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncle Sam stands for the United States, where a seesaw is a teeter; the second sense reads the word as players who tee off.
explanation.definitionFit: American English calls a seesaw a teeter, and golfers start each hole from the tee.
